video_title: Crypto Is Rebuilding a Trillion-Dollar Market
gist: Adrian Kechinad, co-founder of the vault curator Steakhouse, walks Bankless through the DeFi vault stack — Morpho-style isolated borrow/lend primitives at the base, curators like Steakhouse and Aave above them, and consumer distributors (Robinhood, Coinbase) on top. His core thesis is that the biggest vault growth will be 'boring': on-chain repo markets against Bitcoin, ETH and stablecoins, replicating a trillions-of-dollars TradFi market, while the high-risk discretionary end (the Stream Finance/Elixir tail) is where Hester Peirce's SEC questions and the unresolved curator/depositor principal-agent problem bite.

themes.theme: Vault stack anatomy: infrastructure, curators, distributors

insights.claim: 'Vault' is as semantically open-ended as 'token' — it spans everything from a minimal Morpho liquidity aggregator to a fully discretionary manager who can wire depositor funds to an EOA, so investors must specify which vault type they mean before assessing risk.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Any 'vault sector' TVL or yield comparison is apples-to-oranges unless segmented by discretion level; underwrite the specific configuration, not the label.
insights.quote: It's it's a it's a word like a token. It depends what you're looking for.

insights.claim: The functional definition of a vault is a token that aggregates liquidity toward a goal, making it the on-chain analogue of an ETF as a liquidity aggregator in traditional finance.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Frames vaults as a direct long-term competitor to the ETF wrapper, which sizes the addressable market far beyond DeFi yield farming.
insights.quote: the vault is an is an abstraction for aggregated liquidity not dissimilar to an ETF.

insights.claim: The vault market has three distinct layers — vault infrastructure (Morpho, Beefy, Veda) at the bottom, curators who express risk opinions in the middle, and consumer distributors at the top — and value capture is contested between the layers.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman (host) and Adrian Kechinad
insights.so_what: Gives investors a map for where margin accrues in the vault value chain and which layer is most defensible.

insights.claim: Vault infrastructure differs by how much operator discretion it permits: Morpho vaults are minimal and governance-light, while a Veda-style vault is a richer execution layer that allows more operator actions and discretion.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Discretion level is the key differentiator to diligence when comparing vault platforms and their regulatory exposure.

insights.claim: The first vaults emerged in DeFi summer with Yearn's smart-contract architecture that let depositors delegate strategy selection, but the category only took off once Morpho arrived.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Historical context showing the category's inflection came from infrastructure design, not yield narratives.

insights.claim: Barrier to entry at the vault layer is effectively zero — anyone who can interact with the Morpho smart contract can print their own vault and be its only depositor — which is both the industry's core innovation and a regulatory design constraint.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Zero switching/creation cost means curator moats are reputational and operational, not technical — expect crowded entry and eventual shakeout.
insights.quote: about Morfo is the barrier to entry is zero essentially. You just need to know how to interact with the smart contract and you can print your own vaults.

insights.claim: Morpho pioneered isolated risk borrow/lend markets, deliberately sacrificing the pooled-model network effects (notably collateral re-hypothecation) that Aave enjoys in exchange for a drastically smaller smart-contract risk surface.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Explains the structural trade-off between the two dominant lending architectures and why they attract different collateral and users.

insights.claim: Vaults exist precisely to recapture the network effects that isolated markets destroy — an individual Morpho Blue borrow position has almost no network effect, but aggregated in a vault it compounds as more depositors enable more loans and a more efficient market.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Network effects — and therefore durable value — accrue at the vault/curator layer, not the isolated market layer.

insights.claim: The DeFi experiments that work best reduce smart contracts to the simplest possible primitive — 'a smart contract as a spreadsheet' that just computes accrued interest — because when smart contracts fail they fail catastrophically.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: A design heuristic for judging which DeFi protocols survive: minimal surface plus recomposability beats governance-heavy monoliths.
insights.quote: Smart contracts are very sensitive infrastructure to build anything on. They can go like when they go wrong, they go very wrong. So, you should you should aim to reduce the risk surface as much as possible.

insights.claim: A single Morpho borrow/lend market targets roughly 90% utilization, leaving only about 10% withdrawable at any time, so a depositor whose position exceeds that slice can be unable to exit in full — a liquidity risk vaults mitigate by spreading across many markets.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Concrete withdrawal-capacity math for anyone sizing a large direct position in an isolated lending market versus a vault.
insights.quote: an individual borrow lend market with a Morpho targets 90% of the liquidity to be borrowed at any given time.

insights.claim: Aave is functionally the largest vault curator in the market — one very big verticalized vault whose governance, collateral onboarding and counterparty mitigants mirror what independent curators do, with the difference that only token holders, not depositors, vote.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder), prompted by host
insights.so_what: Reframes Aave as a competitor to curators rather than a separate category, which changes how to model curator market share and fee compression.
insights.quote: They're the biggest curator for sure. We like to say we are the biggest curator. In reality, Aave is the biggest curator.

insights.claim: Steakhouse's differentiator versus Aave is that it integrates governance with the depositors themselves via an Aragon DAO that gives vault users a veto over proposed collateral onboardings.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Depositor-level veto rights are an emerging competitive feature in curation; watch whether rivals copy it as a trust differentiator.
insights.quote: we build an Aragon DAO around the vault and we make the vault user participate, so to speak.

insights.claim: Curating a repo-style vault is about maximizing market efficiency rather than maximizing yield — the vault succeeds when borrowers and lenders meet faster at a lower spread, not when the APY headline is highest.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Suggests curator value should be benchmarked on spread compression and rebalancing quality, not on advertised APY.

themes.theme: Curator risk framework and collateral onboarding

insights.claim: Steakhouse's risk framework treats collateral onboarding as the single key inflection point — after onboarding there is no active ongoing managerial effort, the market simply settles around the parameters set.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Depositor diligence should concentrate on a vault's onboarding record and proposal process, since that is where nearly all risk is decided.

insights.claim: In a repo market borrowers are seeking risk while lenders are seeking safety, so the curator's job is principal protection through collateral selection rather than yield optimization.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: A clean mental model for evaluating whether a curator's incentives are aligned with lender capital preservation.
insights.quote: borrowers are seeking risk, lenders are seeking safety. We aim to minimize the risk to the principal as much as possible.

insights.claim: The chief lender protection in a vault is the haircut — the loan-to-value cap that forces borrowers to over-collateralize, buying buffer and time for repayment before bad debt accrues.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: LTV parameters are the primary quantitative lever to compare across vaults offering similar collateral.

insights.claim: Credit risk in the asset and risk in the loan position are separable: wrapped Bitcoin is very low credit risk (BitGo-held, highly liquid) yet a market that onboarded it at 98% LTV would still be too risky because the haircut is insufficient to prevent bad debt.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: A concrete worked example showing collateral quality alone doesn't make a market safe — parameters do.
insights.quote: wrapped Bitcoin, we would consider it to to be very low credit risk. It's, you know, held in BitGo. It's very liquid, what have you.

insights.claim: Steakhouse's onboarding bias is toward collateral that is regulated or supervised, or that carries very strong on-chain guarantees, and it audits the governance structure of the underlying token issuer.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Signals which token designs get access to prime curator liquidity — an issuer's governance design directly gates its collateral demand.

insights.claim: Etherfi was upgraded from Steakhouse's 'high yield' bucket toward 'prime' only after it agreed to strip managerial discretion over its token via very long time locks and governance guards around key roles like minter roles.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: A template for token issuers: adding time locks and role guards is a concrete path to cheaper, deeper collateral liquidity from curators.
insights.quote: What we would consider prime is your life needs to be made a lot more difficult.

insights.claim: A curator declining a collateral market is not a risk signal in itself — Steakhouse says many perfectly sound markets go un-onboarded simply for lack of time or domain understanding.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Caution against reading curator absence as a negative credit opinion when screening assets.

insights.claim: Curator business models create structural risk scope creep: because curators earn a cut of the yield flowing through their vault, they are permanently incentivized to raise both TVL and yield, which implicitly raises risk.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman (host)
insights.so_what: The central bear case on the curator business model — monitor fee structures and yield drift as an early warning of risk creep.

insights.claim: The adverse curator incentive only binds if depositors have inelastic risk tolerance and sort purely on APY; Adrian argues events like Stream Finance and Elixir and the 10/10 drawdown have made DeFi users more discerning about underlying exposures.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: If depositor behavior really is shifting from APY-chasing to exposure analysis, conservative curators gain share and yield spreads widen between prime and degen vaults.
insights.quote: my hope is that the the average DeFi user looks at it and then recognizes actually maybe the highest API is not the best because maybe I should be looking into what the underlying exposures are.

insights.claim: The host pushes back that risk assessment cannot be delegated to end users if crypto intends to onboard the world — the tire-kicking function must live somewhere else in the tech stack for the vault industry to scale.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman (host)
insights.so_what: Identifies an unfilled market gap — independent, scalable vault risk ratings/analytics — as a business opportunity in the stack.

insights.claim: Adrian expects curator survivorship to be the real cleansing mechanism: over several cycles the more risk-taking curators die off and in five years the remaining set is whoever made the cumulatively best decisions.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Implies curator market share is a long-duration reputation trade — back operators with clean multi-cycle records.

insights.claim: Repo-style vaults do not require exotic collateral to succeed — the discipline is doing a few things well rather than putting Stream- or Elixir-style exposures into the book.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Sets an explicit red line investors can use to screen vault holdings for mandate drift.
insights.quote: You don't need to be putting in exotic stream elixir stuff. You just need to do few things well.

insights.claim: Vaults embed a live principal-agent problem: curators take a performance fee on yield but lose only future fees if a vault is exploited, while depositors lose principal — an asymmetry that is muted for BTC/ETH over-collateralized vaults and severe for high-yield, low-liquidity repo markets.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman (host) and Adrian Kechinad
insights.so_what: The asymmetry scales with vault risk — price curator fees against loss-absorbing capacity, not just APY.

insights.claim: Steakhouse allocates its entire company treasury to its own vaults and has made a public commitment to absorb losses, but both parties agree this is a social commitment, not a structural or cryptographically enforced fix.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Skin-in-the-game commitments are a partial mitigant investors should verify on-chain, but they do not substitute for enforceable first-loss capital.
insights.quote: That's why we made this public commitment of like look, our whole treasury is in our vaults.

insights.claim: Bad debt in vaults can accrue disproportionately to depositors who exit last, creating a structural bank-run dynamic where early exiters leave whole and stayers face growing impairment.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: A design flaw with direct trading implications: at the first sign of impairment the rational move is to exit immediately, which accelerates the run.
insights.quote: You can have an instance where it accrues the most to the people who leave last, which is sub-optimal, right?

insights.claim: Curators do face real economic consequences for losses through destroyed brand equity — some have gone from leading the pack to completely shutting down — but that penalty is abstract and returns nothing to the depositor who lost principal.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Reputational discipline is real but non-compensatory; the market still lacks a recovery mechanism for impaired depositors.

insights.claim: Adrian argues the required backstop should scale with discretion: fully discretionary vaults should carry cryptographically enforced buffers, surplus, insurance or third-party supervision, while a prime vault lending only against BTC and ETH probably does not need one.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Points to a coming market for vault insurance/slashing backstops targeted at the discretionary end of the spectrum.
insights.quote: we prefer cryptographic mechanisms to social ones. Social ones have value, but they are imperfect when compared to a cryptographic one.

themes.theme: Where the TVL goes: boring on-chain repo at trillions of scale

insights.claim: Adrian expects the boring, low-risk vaults to grow more and faster than the high-risk end, because vault infrastructure's benefits are strongest at scale.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Directs capital allocation toward prime/repo-style vault infrastructure rather than the high-APY tail.
insights.quote: This is not going to be super exciting but we expect the more boring vaults to grow more and faster.

insights.claim: There is a striking build-order asymmetry in DeFi: on-chain regulated hedge funds already run on vault infrastructure at the extreme risk end, yet there is still no efficient overnight repo market for US Treasuries on chain.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Names the single largest unbuilt primitive in on-chain finance — an on-chain Treasury repo market — as the biggest near-term opportunity.
insights.quote: but we don't have a very efficient overnight repo market for US Treasuries on chain.

insights.claim: The prize Steakhouse is targeting is the trillions of dollars of daily activity that already runs through traditional repo markets, migrated on chain for transparency, accessibility and composability rather than for higher yield.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Sizes the vault opportunity against repo rather than against DeFi TVL, an order-of-magnitude larger framing.
insights.quote: we are talking about trillions and trillions of dollars worth of activity that takes place on repo markets today.

insights.claim: The host frames the trajectory as crypto rebuilding the repo markets — the true basement of finance — on chain with stablecoins and pristine collateral like Bitcoin and ETH, with Apollo and BlackRock as the incoming allocators.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman (host)
insights.so_what: If TradFi allocators enter via prime collateral repo vaults, demand for BTC/ETH as collateral and for stablecoin liquidity compounds structurally.
insights.quote: we're rebuilding repo markets on chain, more efficiently with uh stablecoins and pristine collateral like Bitcoin and ETH.

insights.claim: The host identifies the unanswered second-order question as what emerges for the on-chain economy and for Bitcoin itself once repo-scale stablecoin and institutional flows arrive on chain.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman (host)
insights.so_what: Flags a research gap worth front-running: the reflexive effect of on-chain repo scale on crypto-native asset economics.

insights.claim: Crypto guarantees can make a constrained on-chain vault safer than a hedge fund because the operator can be cryptographically prevented from straying from mandate — whereas the TradFi graveyard is full of hedge funds that did exactly that.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: The strongest argument for institutional adoption of vaults over fund wrappers: enforceable mandate constraints, not higher yield.
insights.quote: graveyard of TradFi is littered with dead hedge funds that strayed from their mandate or took more risk.

insights.claim: The flip side of cryptographic finality is total loss: transferring stablecoins into a black box like Stream Finance means the funds are gone and managerial discretion is fully surrendered.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: The same property that enables enforcement makes opaque vaults uniquely unrecoverable — a reason to require on-chain transparency of positions.
insights.quote: when you transfer stable coins into a black box like Stream Finance, then it's gone

insights.claim: Trustlessness and permissionlessness are framed not as ideology but as market-efficiency tools that lower search costs, frictions and spreads, letting vaults find equilibrium faster by aggregating liquidity.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Reframes the DeFi pitch for institutional audiences in terms of spread compression rather than censorship resistance.
insights.quote: the trustlessness and permissionlessness are a way of improving market efficiency. This is uh like this benefits everyone through lower search costs, lower frictions, lower spreads.

themes.theme: SEC, Hester Peirce and 'internet-native asset management'

insights.claim: Hester Peirce's recent memo asks whether vault curators are effectively asset managers engaged in securities-like activity, and Steakhouse treats it as thoughtful and intends to take up her invitation to talk rather than resist it.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Regulatory posture toward curation is being set now; curators that engage early are likelier to define the standard.
insights.quote: I think Hester's memo was very thoughtful. Uh you know, we'll certainly take her up on the invitation and go and have a chat.

insights.claim: Adrian concedes vault curation is a type of asset management but calls it 'internet-native asset management' — similar to existing wrappers yet new in meaningful ways that deserve fresh regulatory treatment.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: The industry's framing for regulators; if it sticks, it defines a new registration category rather than forcing curators into fund rules.
insights.quote: It is a type of asset management, sure. We call it like internet-native asset management. It's similar, but it's new in meaningful ways, and so it's worth a second look.

insights.claim: Low risk does not equal outside securities law — Adrian says even so-called low-risk vaults retain managerial discretion and can be configured in ways that either comply with or violate securities laws.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Contradicts the assumption that conservative prime vaults are automatically safe from regulatory action; configuration is what matters.

insights.claim: Steakhouse is willing to simply register with the SEC if a conversation reveals its activities are covered, arguing frameworks already exist for players clearly conducting securities activity.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: A credible signal that leading curators will pursue compliance rather than offshore, lowering regulatory tail risk for the prime end of the sector.
insights.quote: I would rather have a chat with the SEC first and confirm that and if there are areas that we need to address we will just register. That's fine.

insights.claim: The gaps Adrian names between vault practice and existing regulation are legal liability, insurance and disclosure regimes — investor protections that feature in regulation today but have no parallel in the pure vault space.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: A checklist of missing infrastructure — vault insurance, disclosure standards and liability wrappers are greenfield businesses.

insights.claim: Adrian argues for tiered standards: not all vaults should meet the same requirements, and any standardization must preserve the ability for an individual to whip up their own vault permissionlessly.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Defines the industry's likely lobbying position — risk-tiered rules rather than a blanket registration regime.

insights.claim: Vault technology could enforce investor protections faster and more securely than courts — legal liability doesn't disappear but can be codified and executed on chain instead of waiting two years for a court settlement.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Reframes compliance as a product feature, the strongest pitch for regulators to bless rather than restrict vault structures.
insights.quote: The legal liability doesn't magically disappear. But it can be codified or enforced in a clearer way with a vault versus waiting for 2 years for a whole court settlement.

insights.claim: The host maps the vault industry's future as two parallel quest lines: scaling low-risk repo vaults toward trillions with institutional collateral, and building legal liability plus consumer protection so the high-risk discretionary end can also scale.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman (host)
insights.so_what: A clean two-track investment map for the sector: infrastructure/collateral plays versus compliance/insurance plays.

themes.theme: Distributors vs curators, consolidation, and the Steakhouse business

insights.claim: Consumer distributors like Robinhood, Coinbase and Kraken own the end-customer relationship and can take a fat cut of vault economics, putting structural fee pressure on the curators sitting behind them.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman (host)
insights.so_what: Distribution, not curation, may capture the majority of retail vault margin — a key question for valuing curator businesses.

insights.claim: Aave is already pushing forward into distribution — building its own savings front end to own the end-to-end customer relationship and compete with Robinhood and Coinbase rather than depend on them.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Signals vertical integration by the largest curator; watch whether Aave's direct consumer product erodes exchange earn-product share.

insights.claim: Adrian's counter-thesis is that curation stays a viable standalone specialty because it is narrow enough and difficult enough that a platform like Coinbase usually won't spend the time to capture the remaining margin in-house.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: The bull case for independent curators rests on operational difficulty, a moat that erodes if tooling commoditizes curation.
insights.quote: It's a sufficiently narrow activity and it's sufficiently difficult or not trivial that it it's often not worth the time to invest to capture the remaining margin for a platform like Coinbase.

insights.claim: Steakhouse explicitly will never try to compete with Robinhood or Coinbase, expecting integration pressure to run the other direction — distributors reaching down into curation rather than curators reaching up into distribution.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Sets expectations for who acquires whom if vault consolidation begins.

insights.claim: Adrian argues vault-management consolidation is still years away because growing industries delay consolidation — the opportunity set is expanding faster than incumbents can close it, leaving niches for new entrants.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Implies a multi-year window for new curator entrants before M&A compresses the field — relevant timing for early-stage bets.
insights.quote: growing industries have a tendency to delay consolidation, uh because there's just more op- there's more opportunity for more people.

insights.claim: Steakhouse claims to have reached a size comparable to Aave as a curator despite not existing two years ago, illustrating how fast share can be taken in the vault market.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: A concrete growth datapoint on curator market structure and how quickly incumbency can be challenged.
insights.quote: Steakhouse has staked a significant claim next to Aave, like we are comparable in size to Aave, and we didn't exist 2 years ago.

insights.claim: Steakhouse is a non-venture-backed family business that measures its plans in centuries, which changes its behavior versus VC-funded competitors chasing an exit.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Ownership structure is a real differentiator in a business where risk discipline compounds over cycles; it also makes acquisition less likely.
insights.quote: Steakhouse has the odd feature that we're not venture-backed. Unlike many businesses in crypto, we're a family business. And so, we like to think in centuries.

insights.claim: Steakhouse's 18-month plan is more of the same — positioning as the product for fintechs and distributors, watching real-world assets enter vaults, and shifting from point farming toward conventional carry trades.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: The points-to-carry rotation is a leading indicator that vault yields will become more fundamentally sourced and more differentiated between vaults.
insights.quote: I'm very happy to move away from point farming and start to move into regular meat and potatoes carry trades.

insights.claim: The shift from points to real yield will increase how much vaults differentiate from one another and increase overall complexity, which is part of why regulators are taking a closer look.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Rising dispersion between vaults means selection skill starts to matter for depositors, favoring curators with real underwriting capability.

insights.claim: Credit risk events are the operational insomnia driver for a curator — Steakhouse monitors vaults, liquidity and collateral continuously across a globally distributed team in Australia, Africa, Hong Kong, the US and Europe.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Underlines that curation is a 24/7 operational business, raising the bar for new entrants and justifying the fee take.
insights.quote: Staked us is a worldwide business, so we have people in Australia and Africa and Hong Kong and the US and Europe.

insights.claim: AI will accelerate vault curation but not replace it — Adrian says he would not use a vault entirely managed by an AI, while Steakhouse's own work is already significantly faster because of AI.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: Expect team-scalability gains rather than headcount replacement; AI-native risk tooling is the investable slice, not autonomous vaults.
insights.quote: but I know for sure at least in our case, our work is significantly accelerated in pace thanks to AI.

insights.claim: Adrian invokes Jevons paradox for AI in vaults: better and cheaper capability accelerates consumption, so AI ends up increasing the total number of vaults rather than shrinking the industry.
insights.speaker: Adrian Kechinad (Steakhouse co-founder)
insights.so_what: If vault count explodes, demand for curation, ratings and risk analytics scales with it rather than being disintermediated.
insights.quote: But, people are hungry for vaults. So, all all it will do is increase the number of vaults.
